title: A yellow leaf (235–238)
hook: you are now like a withered leaf; make yourself an island, work hard, be wise

segments.voice: Yesterday, three doors guarded: body, tongue and mind. Your line was three doors guarded. Did you catch one sharp sentence at the door? Day two hundred four, and chapter eighteen begins: impurity.

Pick up a leaf in late autumn. The yellow ones, the ones that let go of the branch without any wind at all. It's light, dry and a little curled, and it still has every vein in place, like a map of a life. It was green in May. It didn't notice the change until it was nearly done. Most of us are the same. The years feel slow until one day they don't. Chapter eighteen of the Dhammapada opens by holding up a leaf like that and saying, gently but directly, this is you. And then it tells you what to build. Today: a yellow leaf.
screen: `A LEAF IN LATE AUTUMN.` → `GREEN IN MAY.` → `THIS IS YOU.`

segments.voice: Verse two thirty-five, in Max Müller's translation: "Thou art now like a sear leaf, the messengers of death (Yama) have come near to thee; thou standest at the door of thy departure, and thou hast no provision for thy journey." Sear is an old word for dry and withered. The messengers of death, in the Pali, are Yama's men, death's own servants, already standing near. And the image is of someone at the door, about to leave on a long trip, with no packed bag and no food for the road. The old commentary says these verses were spoken to an old man near the end of his life, as a gentle push to make good use of what remained. Then the answer, verse two thirty-six: "Make thyself an island, work hard, be wise!" An island. In a flood, an island is the one piece of ground the water can't cover. The Pali word is dīpa, the word you met on day seventy-nine, when the Buddha, near the end, told Ānanda to be islands to themselves. Island or lamp, it can be read either way. What this verse adds is the building material: effort and wisdom, gathered while there's still time. This isn't meant to frighten anyone. The leaf is simply honest. And a leaf that knows it's a leaf can still do a great deal of good before it lets go.
screen: `A SEAR LEAF AT THE DOOR.` · `NO PROVISION FOR THE JOURNEY.` · `DĪPA — ISLAND, OR LAMP.` · `SOLID GROUND, WHILE THERE'S TIME.` · then, large: `MAKE AN ISLAND.`

segments.voice: Sit, and if you have a leaf nearby, hold it; if not, picture one, yellow and light in your palm. Let yourself feel, without drama, that your time is not endless. Then ask: what's one thing that really matters that I keep putting off? A conversation. A practice. A kindness. A letter. Let it come up on its own. Hold it next to the leaf. Then let both rest, and sit on your island: this breath, this ground, steady in the flood. The bell holds the time.
A yellow leaf. Verse two thirty-five: you are now like a withered leaf, at the door of departure. So, verse two thirty-six: make yourself an island.
Your line: make an island. Today, do the one thing that matters that you've been putting off, or at least its first small step. Day two hundred four.

howItsDone: Buddhists often reflect on death as a spur to practice, and the Buddha's advice to be an island to oneself is often quoted as a call to rely on one's own effort and the teaching.

match.prompt: match each image to its meaning.

myth: dīpa in Pali can mean both island and lamp
translators still weigh which to use; both fit the image.
these verses are meant to frighten people about death
the commentary sets them as a gentle push to use the time that's left.
Müller's 'sear leaf' means a dry, withered leaf
sear is an old word for dry and withered.

fork.setup: you're standing at the door of a long journey, and you realize you have nothing packed. what does verse 236 say to do?
options: make yourself an island: work hard, be wise.
sit down and wait for someone to pack for you.
fork.reveal: "make thyself an island, work hard, be wise!" solid ground in the flood, built while there's time.

original.note: Pali: island, and also lamp — so karohi dīpam attano, make an island for yourself.

trapdoor: what you thought: life is short, so hurry.
what it means: you're like a leaf in autumn, so build solid ground now, from effort and wisdom.
what a scholar hears: Müller's 'messengers of death (Yama)' renders yamapurisā, Yama's men; dīpa can be read as island (Sanskrit dvīpa) or lamp (Sanskrit dīpa).
